description:
FILED s410 (Opus 5) by #341's measurement of t/op/lexsub.t.  This is what the
~139 unmeasured rows of that file sit behind, and it is a MIS-COMPILE, not a
missing feature: PCL reads the indirect-object method call as a function call
with a function-call argument.

    sub F::h { 4242 }
    our sub h { 4343 }
    print h F;          # perl: 4242 (= F->h)   PCL: undefined function pl-F

    emission:  (pl-h (let ((*wantarray* t)) (pl-F)))

perl's own rule is NOT a guess and PCL can apply the same one: a bareword after
a callable word is an indirect OBJECT (a class name) only when it is not itself
a declared sub.  Probed both ways vs perl 5.40.3:

    sub F { 7 } sub F::h { 4242 } sub h { 4343 }; print h F;
    perl: 4343      PCL: 4343      <- AGREE; a declared sub wins, in both

    (no `sub F`)     sub F::h { 4242 } our sub h { 4343 }; print h F;
    perl: 4242      PCL: crash     <- the divergence

So the discriminator is exactly "is there a sub of that name in scope", which
is #266's callable classifier, already in the tree.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND ONE FILE: with no `sub F` the failure is LOUD (undefined
function).  With one it is not reached.  But the shape `WORD BAREWORD` where
the bareword is a KNOWN PACKAGE and no sub of that name exists is silent-wrong
territory the moment the called sub tolerates its argument -- `new Foo(...)`,
the classic indirect-object constructor, is the same grammar.

MEASUREMENT (s410, t/op/lexsub.t):
    perl 156/0     PCL 7/10, then the file DIES at row 18
    row 18 = `is((h F),4242, 'our sub symbol translation does not affect meth
    names')`, op/lexsub.t:91 -- the first `h F`.
    139 of perl's 156 rows are behind it.  Drops in that file: 12 (was 14
    before #376).

WHERE IT BELONGS: docs/option-b-phase2-plan.md lists "indirect object" under
Track A (#371) as a feature ABSENCE to turn into a ruled refusal.  That is not
enough for this file: a refusal DIES too, and the file would still abort at row
18.  To recover the 139 rows the statement must become a counted DROP (file
mode continues) or the call must be LOWERED as `F->h`.  Lowering is the better
answer and it is small once the term grammar can say "this bareword is not
callable": `WORD BAREWORD ARGS?` -> `BAREWORD->WORD(ARGS)`.  Sequence it with
#372/#343 (the operand-grammar work), not before -- and note the s409 ruling
that turning a crash-form into a counted drop is a legal census INCREASE, so
the drop route is available as an interim step if the grammar work slips.

BAR: the two probes above (both directions) plus `new Foo(1,2)`,
`print STDERR "x"` (a filehandle bareword, which must NOT become a method
call), `h F::G` and a bareword that is a known package AND a declared sub.
op/lexsub.t back above 17 rows is the measurement that says it worked.

Related: #341 (the sizing that found it), #371 (Track A refusals), #372/#343
(the operand grammar), #266 (the callable classifier that is the discriminator).


s425 (Fable, 2026-08-22): the USER decided indirect object syntax is MAYBE LATER (docs/not-supported.md "Indirect object syntax with a SCALAR invocant").  This task STAYS OPEN as the mis-compile record (`h F` -> (pl-h (pl-F)), dies undefined function; perl F->h); its fix is the implementation, cheapest after B3 (#153).  Not scheduled.
subject: Indirect-object method call `h F` compiles to `h(F())` — a CRASH (undefined pl-F) where perl calls F->h; 139 of op/lexsub.t's 156 rows sit behind it. perl's own discriminator (is there a declared sub of that name) is #266's classifier
